# Sela Sutta (MN 92 (PTS MN ii 146))

**ID:** MN 92 (PTS MN ii 146)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)

**Title (English, from literature):** With Sela

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sela Sutta* (MN 92) recounts the conversion of the brahmin Sela and his assembly of pupils [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017]. In the narrative framework, the ascetic Keṇiya prepares an elaborate meal for the Buddha and the Saṅgha [SuttaCentral; Katre 1931]. Observing these preparations, the brahmin Sela approaches the Buddha and inspects him for the thirty-two bodily marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa*) [SuttaCentral; Kingsbury 2002]. When the Buddha miraculously reveals the two marks that are concealed—his tongue and his sheath-covered private parts—Sela is convinced and extols the Buddha in verse [Anālayo 2017; Kingsbury 2002; Katre 1931]. Urging the Buddha to rule as a universal monarch or "king of kings" (*rājābhirāja*), Sela hears the Buddha declare his spiritual kingship as the Dhamma-king; Sela and his followers subsequently go forth and attain arahantship [Endo 1997; Anālayo 2017].

Scholars have given particular attention to the literary composition and transmission of the discourse. The text is virtually identical to the sutta of the same name found in the *Sutta Nipāta* (Snp 3.7) [Kingsbury 2002; Winternitz 1933]. Because of this complete duplication, English translations of the Majjhima Nikāya note that page citations embedded in MN 92 sometimes refer to the PTS pagination of the *Sutta Nipāta* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The verses are also preserved in the *Theragāthā* (Thag 16.6) as the *Selattheragāthā* [Endo 1997; DharmaNexus]. S. M. Katre identified the sutta as a composite work fusing the prose story of Keṇiya—also found in the Vinaya's *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6)—with twenty-four additional stanzas containing the dialogue with Sela [Katre 1931]. In Sanskrit Buddhist literature, the text was known as the *Śailagāthā* and was counted among the preserved poetic collections, as evidenced by citations in the *Divyāvadāna* [Lamotte 1988; Hazra 1994].

SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus document widespread parallels and text reuse for MN 92 across early Buddhist traditions. Full and partial parallels exist in Snp 3.7, the Vinaya *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), the Chinese Vinaya (*dg-kd7*), the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* (*lo-mvu108*), the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 49.6), and the *Itivuttaka* (Iti 100) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies massive Pali-internal reuse with Snp 3.7 (over 22,000 matching characters) and Kd 6 (over 15,000 characters), as well as formulaic descriptions of the thirty-two marks shared with the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3), *Brahmāyu Sutta* (MN 91), and *Lakkhaṇa Sutta* (DN 30) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language matches connect the sutta to the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Lalitavistara*, the Tibetan *Vinayavastu*, and the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* and *Ekottarika-āgama* [DharmaNexus]. In comparative studies, Anālayo notes that the *Ekottarika-āgama* parallel to the sutta illustrates the mark of the retractile organ with the comparison to a king of horses, explaining it as a symbol of chastity and purity [Anālayo 2017].
